narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 61.7% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Placing in the second decile is substantially lower than the average of roughly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted. Your first-year ranking in the third decile also pulled the prediction in the same direction, though less strongly. These two early indicators of how you performed relative to your classmates outweighed everything else.

Your family income, which falls in the upper-middle bracket, was the only notable factor that nudged the prediction slightly toward passing. However, its influence was much smaller than the effect of your class rankings.

Taken together, the model concluded that your academic record in law school made success on the bar exam less likely than the typical accepted applicant.

What you should do next is focus on improving your study approach for the bar exam itself. Many students in similar academic positions raise their chances significantly by enrolling in a structured bar-prep course, forming a consistent study schedule, and practicing timed essay and multiple-choice questions. Re-taking key classes or seeking academic support before attempting the exam again may also help strengthen the record that future applications will review.
